name: Legionarii Britones seniores (palatina)

abilities.name: Testudo
abilities.text: The troops of this unit raise their shields above their heads in a defensive formation.

abilities.name: Spear Wall
abilities.text: The unit moves into close wall formation.

abilities.name: Square
abilities.text: The unit moves into a close square formation. Note that it cannot move whilst this ability is active.

abilities.name: Shield Screen
abilities.text: The unit raises their shields in a static defensive formation.

attributes.name: Disciplined
attributes.text: This unit does not suffer a morale penalty when the general dies. It can also rally after routing more often.

attributes.name: Formation Attack
attributes.text: The unit will try to stay in formation when in melee.

attributes.name: Hide (forest)
attributes.text: This unit can hide in forests until enemy units get too close.

attributes.name: Immune to Fear
attributes.text: This unit is immune to the fear effects of scary units.

short: The name Britones clearly indicates a British origin of the unit. First of all, Britones refers to the Britons, i.e. the native Celtic population of Britain before the conquest of the island by the Anglo-Saxons. In this sense, it is clear that the Britones (seniores) unit was originally formed from the Britons, i.e. in the territory of Britain, and then transferred to Europe, to the lower Danube. Of the events of late Roman military history of the late 4th century AD, which concerned the territory of Britain, we can highlight only the rebellion of Magnus Maximus, the usurper who proclaimed himself emperor in 383 just on the territory of Britain. The Brittonic monk and historian Gildas, who lived in the 6th century, mentions that having seized power in Britain, Magnus Maximus headed to Gaul «accompanied by a large horde of associates». E. Chrysos came to the conclusion that the main part of Magnus Maximus' army was formed by the young Britons, whom the usurper recruited into his army when he was still on the territory of Britain: the phrase ingens iuventas («a great number of young men») from Gildas can be interpreted as a reference to the local Celtic population of Britain. Therefore, we can assume that the Britones unit was formed from young Britons in 383, and that the name Britones itself represented the ethnic composition of the unit.
history: In the face of an increasing number of barbarian incursions, the effective defence of Rome’s now-sprawling territory became a serious problem in the 4th century AD. The Emperor Constantine’s controversial solution was to divide the army into two halves. 'Limitanei', literally ‘the men on the limes’ or 'borders', were frontier garrison troops intended to pin down an invading force until the full-time 'comitatenses', the late-Roman equivalent of the traditional Legionaries, could arrive to deal with the situation decisively. Although well-equipped, limitanei were generally considered by all to be second-class warriors. This was possibly because they were often part-time soldiers who had been encouraged to settle and farm the land around their outposts in exchange for policing the Empire's borders.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
